blocks.prompt: The Little Tube That Measures Heat
blocks.text: A thermometer is a tool. It measures how hot or how cold something is. Most thermometers have a thin glass tube with colored liquid inside. Heat makes the liquid spread out and take up more room. So the liquid climbs up the tube. Cold makes the liquid squeeze together. So the liquid slides back down. The numbers on the side tell you the temperature. Water turns to ice at zero degrees Celsius. Water boils at one hundred degrees Celsius. Your body sits at about thirty-seven degrees. A thermometer does not make you warm. It only tells you the truth about heat.

blocks.prompt: Why the Red Line Climbs
blocks.text: A thermometer works because of one simple habit of matter: almost everything gets a little bigger when it warms up, and a little smaller when it cools down. Scientists call this thermal expansion. Look closely at a glass thermometer. At the bottom is a small round bulb full of liquid. Rising out of the bulb is a tube with a hole through the middle so thin you can barely see it. When the bulb warms, the liquid inside swells. It has nowhere to go but up that skinny tube. Because the tube is so narrow, a tiny bit of swelling in the bulb becomes a long climb up the glass. That is the trick. The thin tube turns a change too small to notice into a change you can read from across the room. Cool the bulb and the liquid shrinks back down. The numbers printed beside the tube let you name exactly where it stopped. Without those numbers, you would only know that today is warmer than yesterday. With them, you can say how much.

blocks.prompt: Building a Ruler for Heat
blocks.text: For most of human history, nobody could say how hot anything was. You could say a day felt warm or a soup felt too hot to eat, but feelings are not measurements. Two people standing in the same room will disagree about it, and both of them are right about what they feel. Around 1592, Galileo built a device called a thermoscope. It was a glass bulb on an upside-down tube standing in water. As the air in the bulb warmed and expanded, it pushed the water down. The thing worked, but it had no numbers on it. It could tell you that something had changed. It could not tell you how much. The missing piece was a scale, and a scale needs fixed points: two temperatures that are always the same, anywhere, that you can mark and then divide up. Daniel Fahrenheit found his in the 1720s. He built the first reliable mercury thermometer, then set his zero at the coldest temperature he could reliably make, a slush of ice, water, and salt. Anders Celsius chose better anchors in 1742: the freezing point of water and its boiling point, with one hundred steps between them. Oddly, Celsius put zero at boiling and one hundred at freezing. Other scientists flipped his scale around after he died, and the flipped version is the one on your wall today. That is the whole invention. Not the glass, not the liquid, but the agreement. Once two people in different countries marked the same two fixed points, they could finally compare notes. A number replaced an opinion, and science could start measuring weather, fevers, engines, and stars.

notes: Heat always flows from hotter to colder

A digital thermometer measures electrical resistance

blocks.prompt: What a Thermometer Actually Measures
blocks.text: Here is a strange fact about the tool on your wall. A thermometer never measures the temperature of the room. It only ever measures the temperature of itself. Think about what happens when you put a thermometer in a glass of water. Heat always flows from the warmer thing into the cooler thing, never the other way. If the water is warmer than the glass bulb, energy moves into the bulb. The liquid inside swells and rises. It keeps rising until the bulb and the water are equally hot, which is the point where the flow stops. Scientists call that thermal equilibrium. Once it arrives, the thermometer has become the same temperature as the water, and reading the thermometer is the same as reading the water. This is why you have to wait. Pull it out early and you are reading a number that has not finished happening yet. It also explains a rule that catches people out. The thermometer must be small compared to whatever you are measuring, because it does not just read the water, it changes it. A cold bulb steals a little heat from the glass on its way to matching it. With a bathtub, that theft is far too small to matter. With a single drop, the thermometer could easily win. So what is temperature, underneath? Everything is built from particles that are constantly jiggling, and temperature is a measure of how vigorously they jiggle on average. Hot means fast. Cold means slow. Heat is the energy that moves between things because of that difference. Temperature is not the same as heat. A sparkler burns at a far higher temperature than a bathtub full of warm water, yet the bathtub holds vastly more heat, because heat depends on how much stuff there is. Modern thermometers exploit different habits of matter to catch the same jiggling. A digital thermometer contains a thermistor, a component whose electrical resistance changes in a predictable way as it warms, so the reading is really a measurement of electricity. An infrared thermometer does not touch anything at all. Every object gives off invisible infrared light, and warmer objects give off more of it, so the device reads the glow and works backward to a number. Different tricks, one job: turning something you can only feel into something everyone can agree on.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Absolute zero is minus 273.15 degrees Celsius
Kelvin proposed his scale in 1848
Fahrenheit's zero was a bucket of salty slush
98.6 F is a rounded 37 C, converted
Carl Wunderlich took roughly a million readings
Mercury thermometers are being phased out because mercury is toxic

blocks.prompt: The Instrument That Only Ever Talks About Itself
blocks.text: Ask someone what a thermometer does and they will tell you it measures how hot something is. That answer is wrong in an interesting way, and the error is worth chasing, because it leads directly to one of the strangest ideas in physics. Begin with the machinery. A classic glass thermometer is a bulb of liquid joined to a tube whose channel is finer than a hair. Nearly all matter expands when heated, and the liquid in the bulb expands considerably more than the glass around it, so warmth forces it into the only escape available, the thin bore above. Because that channel is so narrow, a swelling far too small to see becomes a column you can read at a glance. The instrument is not sensitive. It is an amplifier. Now the correction. When you slide a thermometer into a cup of tea, it does not somehow inspect the tea. Energy simply flows from the hotter body to the colder one, as energy always does, until the two bodies stop differing and the flow ends. That state is called thermal equilibrium. The reading you finally take is the thermometer's own temperature, and it is useful only because the thermometer has, by then, become the tea. This is why an impatient reading is a false one, and why a thermometer must be small next to the thing it measures. It always takes a little of what it reports. The physics beneath is stranger still. Temperature is not a substance. It is a statement about motion: the average kinetic energy of the particles in a thing, which is to say how hard they are jiggling. Push that idea to its end and you get a floor. There is a point at which the jiggling reaches its minimum and cannot be reduced further, and no colder temperature exists below it. That floor is absolute zero, minus 273.15 degrees Celsius. Lord Kelvin proposed building a scale from it in 1848. His scale begins at the only zero in the whole business that means anything: zero on the Celsius scale is a memory of freezing water, and zero on the Fahrenheit scale is a memory of a bucket of salty slush in a Dutch workshop in the 1720s, but zero on the Kelvin scale is the actual end of the road. Every scale carries this kind of human fingerprint. Consider the most famous temperature most people know: 98.6 degrees Fahrenheit, normal body heat. It comes from Carl Wunderlich, a German physician who in the 1860s published an average body temperature near 37 degrees Celsius, drawn from roughly a million readings taken from some twenty-five thousand patients with a thermometer a foot long that took twenty minutes to settle. Converted into Fahrenheit, a rounded number in one language became a suspiciously precise number in another, and 98.6 has been quoted ever since as though it were a law. Modern studies of large populations put the average slightly lower and note that it drifts with your age, your activity, and the time of day. The decimal was never a fact about bodies. It was an accident of translation. So the humble tube deserves more respect than it gets. It made feelings into numbers, and numbers can be compared, argued with, and checked by a stranger on the other side of the world. Before it, everyone lived in a private climate of their own sensations, warm or cold according to who was asking. What the thermometer measures is only itself. What it gives us is everything else.
